title: Deciding on the Time to Decide
author: Admired Leadership
summary: When a team faces genuine uncertainty and neither acting nor waiting feels right, this article suggests a third option: deciding when a decision will be made, rather than what the decision will be. Setting a concrete timeline for a future decision reduces the pressure to act prematurely while still giving the organization a structured deadline, decision gates, and criteria to work toward in the meantime. The author argues this approach prevents the paralysis and anxiety that comes from open-ended waiting, because people stop second-guessing inaction once they know a decision point has been set. The piece closes by framing this as a distinct leadership skill — creating clarity about timing even when the underlying facts remain unclear.
points: When uncertainty makes an immediate decision unwise, leaders can still act by setting a firm timeline for when the decision will be made.
A decision schedule reduces ambiguity, mobilizes commitment, and gives the team defined tasks (data-gathering, decision gates) to pursue while waiting.
Announcing a timeline stops team members from second-guessing inaction and refocuses them on daily work.
quotes: Leaders who succumb to the pressure to “do something” — to act decisively — typically regret it later.
When leaders and groups are faced with so much uncertainty that they can’t act, the wise choice is to decide on the time to decide .
A decision schedule reduces ambiguity, mobilizes commitment, and puts people at ease.
Once team members throughout the organization know a timeline for decision-making has been set, they stop second-guessing the inaction
Deciding on the time to decide is one of the most important choices leaders and teams make when confronting a quicksand of uncertainty.
